column4: It sets following Allah's رضوان against returning burdened with His سخط, the section's central rıza/gazap fork cast as two opposed destinations.

The section's quoted manna-and-quail scene makes provision and restraint precede the warning that Allah's غضب may يَحِلّ "upon" its recipients; it is the clearest realization of the descending thing in 1:7.

Immediately after the fall under wrath in 20:81, forgiveness is promised to the repentant, faithful, righteous person who is then guided; it supplies the other end of the section's fall-versus-guidance contrast.
Moses says he hastened to his Lord "so that You may be pleased" (لِتَرْضَى); his movement toward rıza frames the calf episode and his angry return in the following passage.
This one ayah joins Moses' return غضبان أسفا with his question whether the people wanted wrath from their Lord to descend upon them, directly joining the angry face and the falling verdict.
Hud tells his people that defilement and غضب from their Lord have already fallen upon them; it repeats the section's spatial image of wrath landing on a people.
Moses returns to his people غضبان أسفا. It is the parallel bodily scene to 20:86 for the section's dictionary sense of anger visible in a person.
Those who took the calf are promised غضب from their Lord and humiliation. The paired burden makes the section's wrath-and-lowliness reading concrete.
When Moses' anger subsides, the tablets yield guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord. Its cooling of anger leads into the guided side of the contrast.
They follow what angers Allah and hate His رضوان. This is the section's rıza/gazap opposition stated as two rival courses of action.
Allah's curse and غضب are joined to being farther astray from the level path. It directly confirms the section's meeting of wrath with losing the way.
Allah guides those who follow His رضوان to paths of peace and ultimately a straight path. It makes the favorable side of 1:7 a route, not merely a verdict.
It names the people whom Allah has favored (أَنْعَمَ) and calls prophets, truthful ones, martyrs, and righteous people beautiful companions, exactly developing the section's shared road.
The people Allah favored are also those guided and chosen; upon hearing the signs they fall prostrate and weeping. It joins favor, guidance, and the section's face-to-ground response.
Those seeking Allah's فضل and رضوان bear a mark on their faces from prostration. It is the section's strongest meeting of favorable pursuit, face, and worship.
The ayah explicitly joins cooled eyes, absence of grief, and being pleased with what is given. It realizes the section's dictionary sense of the eye's نعمة as calmness alongside rıza.
Allah does not approve disbelief but approves gratitude. This gives the section's hamd/ni'ma side an ethical opposite to divine displeasure.
The tranquil soul is commanded to return to its Lord راضية مرضية, a final reciprocal rıza that reverses the section's falling wrath.
The Garden's people receive the formula "Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him," giving the favorable community its final mutual rıza.
On the Day when truthfulness benefits the truthful, Allah says He is pleased with them and they with Him. It joins the section's yawm of judgment to its favorable face.
The first Emigrants, Helpers, and those who follow them well receive Allah's rıza and the Garden; the verse supplies another defined company on the favored course.
Allah's party are those with faith written in their hearts; He is pleased with them and they with Him. It defines a community by the reciprocal rıza opposite the wrath-marked groups.
Allah is pleased with the believers at the pledge, knows what is in their hearts, and sends tranquility. It shows rıza arriving with an inward, calming effect rather than rage.
After gardens, rivers, and good dwellings, the ayah says Allah's رضوان is greater. It treats rıza as the crowning favorable gift.
Some are pleased when given charity and become angry when not given it. The verse makes receiving a gift visibly divide rıza from its opposite, in a human and morally exposed form.
It tells the dissatisfied to be content with what Allah and His Messenger gave and to await further فضل. It clarifies the proper response to the gift in 9:58.
People may seek the believers' pleasure, but Allah does not approve the defiantly disobedient. The boundary distinguishes human appeasement from the rıza that matters in the section.
Allah completes His نعمة and says He has approved Islam as religion. It joins the section's active bestowal of favor to explicit divine rıza.
Solomon asks to be grateful for the نعمة bestowed on him and his parents and to do a righteous deed Allah approves. Gratitude turns favor toward rıza.
The human who recognizes parental burden asks to be grateful for Allah's favor and to act in a way He approves. It repeats the section's favor-to-rıza relation in a lived appeal.
Abraham is grateful for Allah's favors; Allah chooses him and guides him to a straight path. The verse directly fuses ni'ma, gratitude, election, and the road of 1:6–7.
Forgiveness, the completion of Allah's نعمة, and guidance to a straight path occur together. It gives the favored course the same direction the section finds after wrath's fall.
Faith's lovers are the rightly guided in 49:7, and this ayah calls that state a فضل and نعمة from Allah. It makes guidance itself a bestowed favor.
The command repeatedly turns faces toward the Sacred Mosque so that Allah may complete His favor and guide the community. It joins face, نعمة, and guidance in one direction.
Garden-dwellers say praise belongs to Allah who guided them; they confess they could not have been guided without Him. Their hamd is the speech of the favored, guided side.
The command to glorify with the Lord's حمد is paired with "perhaps you will be pleased." It binds the section's hamd and rıza in the same address.
Allah returns Moses to his mother so that her eye may be cooled and she will not grieve. This is the section's exact Quranic counterpart to the eye's نعمة as settled coolness.
Pharaoh's wife calls the rescued infant a قرة عين, a coolness of the eye. The scene gives the section's calm eye image a concrete gift and rescue.
Moses is returned to his mother so that her eye may be cooled, her grief cease, and she know Allah's promise true. Favor here visibly repairs the eye's sorrow.
Mary is told to eat, drink, and cool her eye. Provision and an eye made calm appear together, just as the section places ni'ma in the softened face.
The servants ask for spouses and descendants to be قرة أعين. It extends the section's eye-coolness from a private rescue to a hoped-for household gift.
A hidden reward is described as قرة أعين. The section's cool, quiet eye becomes a promised form of favor beyond present sight.
Israel is told to enter, eat abundantly, enter the gate prostrating, and ask for remission; forgiveness and increase await the doers of good. It binds plentiful favor, a bowed face, and pardon.
The wrongdoers alter the commanded word, so a punishment is sent down upon them from heaven. It reverses 2:58's gift and remission with a descending consequence.
The parallel command grants plentiful food, requires entry prostrating, and promises forgiveness and increase. It repeats the section's gift, face-to-ground, and mercy pattern.
Those who wrong the command receive a punishment sent down from heaven. Its descent is the adverse counterpart to the granted abundance in 7:161.
Cloud shade, manna, quail, and the command to eat good provision repeat the provision scene quoted by the section before 20:81's warning.
The cloud, manna, quail, and good provision recur for Israel; their self-wronging supplies the moral pressure behind the section's warning against transgression in a gift.
Before 20:81, Allah recalls saving Israel from its enemy and sending down manna and quail. This ayah supplies the rescue and provision that make the subsequent wrath warning sharp.
After rejecting the given food for lesser substitutes, Israel receives abasement and returns with غضب upon غضب. It makes misuse of provision lead to the section's falling wrath and lowliness.
Those who reject Allah's revelation out of envy return with غضب upon غضب. The repeated burdened return sharpens the section's language of wrath as an acquired descent.
Humiliation is struck upon them and they return with غضب from Allah. The verse visually couples wrath with the lowly condition that the section finds in the adverse face.
Deliberate murder brings Allah's غضب, curse, and Hell. It gives the wrath category an explicit judgmental consequence rather than a passing human emotion.
One who turns away in battle, except for tactical reasons, returns with غضب from Allah and has Hell as destination. The verb of return makes wrath the opposite end of a path.
After faith, a deliberately opened breast to disbelief incurs Allah's غضب and a great punishment. It defines a moral turning that reaches the anger side of the section.
Those who dispute Allah after response has come have void proof, wrath upon them, and severe punishment. It is another collective under the named غضب verdict.
Hypocritical men and women who expect evil of Allah receive the evil turn, curse, and His غضب. The verse locates wrath within a self-confirming hostile stance.
Believers are told not to ally themselves with a people Allah is angry with. It treats divine غضب as a boundary that defines a group, as in 1:7.
Their alliances are called an evil advance because Allah is displeased with them and they remain in punishment. سخط supplies the section's close antonymic field for غضب.
Those given knowledge fall on their chins in prostration when the Quran is recited. It repeats 19:58's favored response as a bodily lowering of the face.
They fall on their chins weeping and it increases them in humility. This is the same prostration-and-tears scene the section attaches to those granted guidance.
When reminded of the signs, believers fall prostrate, glorify with their Lord's حمد, and avoid arrogance. It joins the section's praise and face-to-ground response.
Moses is ordered to remind his people of the أيام الله. It is the source wording for the section's days that carry both punishment and favor.
Moses immediately makes the Days of Allah concrete by recalling deliverance from Pharaoh. It gives 14:5 a saved people before the later warning and gratitude test.
Gratitude brings increase while ingratitude meets severe punishment. It makes the section's gift-versus-adverse-descent division a response to نعمة.
Those who do not expect the أيام الله are set beside the coming recompense for what each people earned. It makes the section's "days" a horizon of judgment as well as remembered events.
A violent wind is sent upon 'Ad in days of misfortune so they taste humiliating punishment. It realizes the section's dictionary explanation of Allah's days as descending punishment on 'Ad.
A screaming wind is sent upon 'Ad on a day of persistent misfortune. This is a concentrated scene of an adverse day arriving over a people.
The destructive wind is imposed on 'Ad for seven nights and eight days. It gives temporal extension to the section's days that bear a punitive descent.
When Allah's command came, Hud and believers with him were saved by mercy from a harsh punishment. It supplies the pardon-and-rescue side of the 'Ad days named in the section.
When Allah's command came, Salih and believers were saved by mercy from that day's humiliation. It gives Thamud the same day, mercy, and abasement pattern.
A secure, richly provided town denies Allah's favors, then tastes a garment of hunger and fear. The verse reverses نعمة into an enclosing bodily affliction.
Eat what Allah has provided, lawful and good, and be grateful for His نعمة. It restates the provision-and-restraint ethic of 20:81 without the transgression.
When Allah bestows favor, the human turns away; when evil touches him, he despairs. This is a direct reversal of the grateful, calm reception of نعمة.
Allah asks why He would punish if people are grateful and believe. It places gratitude on the side opposed to the punitive outcome underlying the section's wrath.
The command to proclaim the Lord's نعمة makes favor answerable in speech, linking the section's ni'ma to its opening language of praise.
After the wrongdoing people are cut off, the declaration is "praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds." It places حمد beside a completed punitive day without making praise into blame.
Abraham praises Allah for granting Ishmael and Isaac in old age. It makes حمد the verbal reception of a particular bestowed gift.
Noah is told to say praise to Allah who saved them from wrongdoing people. It makes deliverance from an adverse collective into a reason for حمد.
David and Solomon receive knowledge and answer with praise to Allah. This gives the section's hamd a grateful response to a recognizable favor.
Those entering the Garden praise Allah for fulfilling His promise and giving them the land. Their حمد belongs to the completed favorable destination.
At the final judgment angels praise their Lord and judgment is made in truth before the praise declaration. It connects the section's hamd to its Day-of-judgment horizon.
The God-fearing call what their Lord sent "good," and the Hereafter's home is described with the praise form نِعْمَ. It realizes the section's dictionary sense of ni'ma as commendation.
Forgiveness and gardens are followed by "excellent is the reward of the workers" (نِعْمَ). The praise-word sense of the section's نعمة marks the favorable verdict.
Allah gives Solomon to David and calls him an excellent servant (نِعْمَ الْعَبْدُ). Bestowal and approval meet in the dictionary sense of ni'ma developed by the section.
The God-fearing restrain anger and pardon people, and Allah loves the doers of good. It gives a human reversal of anger's urge toward retaliation.
Believers avoid grave sins and, when angry, forgive. Its anger-to-forgiveness movement illuminates the section's contrary endings of wrath and pardon.
At remembrance, skins that shiver become soft and hearts soften. This directly extends the section's dictionary image of a thing becoming soft and tender on the favorable side.
Allah protects them from the evil of that Day and gives them radiance and joy. It makes a day of danger end in the bright, eased face opposed to wrath.
The radiance of نعيم is recognized in their faces. It is the closest Quranic realization of the section's softened, blessed face.
Some faces on that Day are ناعمة, from the same ن ع م root as the section's أَنْعَمْتَ. It gives favor a literal facial condition.
That نعمة-marked face is satisfied with its effort (راضية). The ayah makes the favorable face and rıza explicit companions.
Other faces on that Day are humbled. It begins the adverse facial half that the section contrasts with the softened face.
Faces humble themselves before the Living, the Sustainer, while the bearer of wrongdoing fails. It gives the Day's judgment a visible, lowered face.
Fire scorches their faces and leaves them grimacing. This is the bodily extreme of the section's adverse face under divine judgment.
On resurrection day, liars' faces are blackened. It supplies an explicit dark facial sign for the unfavorable verdict.
Eyes are lowered and humiliation covers them; they had been called to prostrate while sound. It reverses the willing prostration of the favored into a marked shame.
They emerge from graves with lowered eyes while humiliation covers them. It repeats the adverse face at the Day they were promised.
On the shaking Day, eyes are lowered. Its direct eye-state belongs with the section's account of emotion and judgment leaving signs around the eye.
Those exposed to Fire are humbled by humiliation and look with a furtive eye. The ayah shows abasement as an eye-and-face posture.
When angels take the disbelievers, they strike their faces and backs. It gives divine rejection a direct injury to the face.
The punitive incursion is sent to disfigure faces and enter the sanctuary. It makes the section's claim that judgment leaves a facial trace concrete in history.
At the birth-news he dislikes, a man's face darkens while he is constricted. It is a human-scale parallel to the section's angry, visibly altered face.
The same darkened, constricted face appears when one is given news of what he ascribes to the Merciful. It reiterates anger or shame taking a facial form.
He frowned (عَبَسَ) and turned away. The section's dictionary gloss of غضوب as frowning finds a direct Quranic facial action, even though the root differs.
Some faces on that Day are radiant. It is the broad eschatological counterpart to the section's favored face.
Those radiant faces look toward their Lord. The ayah completes 75:22's favorable orientation rather than merely naming brightness.
Other faces on that Day are grim. It establishes the direct facial opposite within the same judgment scene.
Those grim faces expect a crushing calamity. It supplies the adverse fate that makes their facial state more than an expression.
Some faces on that Day are bright and shining. This is one of the section's cited favorable facial scenes.
The shining faces are laughing and rejoicing, completing the soft and settled side of the section's contrast.
Other faces have dust upon them. The section explicitly reads this "upon them" as a facial counterpart to 1:7's عَلَيْهِم.
Darkness covers those dust-marked faces. It completes the section's image of an adverse thing descending over the face.
Those who do good receive the best and more; neither dust-darkness nor humiliation covers their faces. It directly negates the covering scene of 80:40–41.
Those who earn evil have faces covered as by pieces of dark night and are humiliated. It is the adverse face that 10:26 excludes for the good-doers.
On the Day, faces are whitened and blackened, and the blackened faces are confronted with their disbelief. It makes the final division visible on the face.
The whitened faces are in Allah's mercy forever. It supplies the mercy-side outcome of the facial division in 3:106.
The unbelievers will be unable to keep Fire from their faces or backs. The face becomes the exposed surface of the adverse judgment.
Those who arrive with evil are thrown face-first into the Fire. It turns the adverse course into a literal downward facial posture.
The one who tries to shield himself from the evil punishment with his face has no protected side left. It is a stark reversal of the face receiving favorable radiance.
They are dragged on their faces into Fire. This physical abasement develops the section's lowly counterpart to the favored face.
A warning threatens to efface faces and turn them backward, or to curse as earlier transgressors were cursed. Facial reversal is joined to the wrath-adjacent curse category.
The blast seizes the wrongdoers of Thamud and leaves them lifeless in their homes. It supplies the punitive side completed by the mercy-and-day rescue of 11:66.
Israel is told to remember the نعمة Allah bestowed and fulfill the covenant. It identifies the same favored people whose provision later meets the warning of wrath.
Allah recalls the نعمة bestowed on Israel and their special favor over peoples. It gives the phrase of bestowed favor a collective historical addressee.
The repeated reminder of Allah's نعمة to Israel keeps the gift before the community that later chooses the calf and receives warnings of غضب.
After water is given from the rock, Israel is told to eat and drink Allah's provision and not spread corruption. It is another gift with a boundary against misuse.
A person gives himself seeking Allah's pleasure (مَرْضَات). It makes rıza a concrete motive for self-offering rather than a detached reward.
Spending seeks Allah's pleasure and is pictured through a fruitful garden. It gives the pursuit of rıza an enacted, nourishing form.
For the God-fearing, gardens and Allah's رضوان are presented as better than worldly desire. It places rıza among the enduring favorable gifts.
Allah's favor turns enemies into brothers by joining their hearts and rescues them from a pit of Fire. Its inner softening and rescue extend the favorable side of the image.
Allah confers favor on believers by sending a messenger who recites, purifies, and teaches. It explains one way divine favor becomes guidance.
Believers return with Allah's favor and bounty, unharmed, having followed His رضوان. It is a positive return set against returning with غضب.
After the companions of those favored in 4:69, the ayah calls that company Allah's فضل. It identifies their companionship as a divine gift.
Private counsel for charity, right, or reconciliation is commended when it seeks Allah's pleasure. The verse gives rıza a socially reparative course.
Purification is followed by Allah's wish to complete His favor so that people may be grateful. It links cleansing, نعمة, and gratitude without the adverse fall.
Moses tells Israel to remember Allah's favor in making prophets and kings among them. It supplies the older gift-history behind the calf and provision narratives.
On hearing revelation, their eyes overflow with tears because they recognize truth. This is an indirect but specific eye-response parallel to 19:58's prostration and weeping.
After the calf episode, those who repent and believe find their Lord forgiving and merciful. It gives a return from the wrath-and-humiliation warning of 7:152.
The Lord announces mercy, His رضوان, and gardens to the believers who migrate and strive. It joins rıza to a promised communal destination.
The final call of Garden-dwellers is praise to Allah. It places حمد at the settled end of the favorable path.
Jacob's eyes turn white from grief. Unlike the section's anger-swollen eye, it is an indirect contrary case showing inner suffering visibly altering the eye.
The arrogant are told to enter Hell, and its dwelling is called بِئْس. It supplies the blame-word that the section explicitly sets opposite the praise-form نِعْمَ.
Gardens of lasting residence complete the "excellent home of the God-fearing" in 16:30. The ayah gives that praise-word its favorable destination.
Allah tells Moses that He had bestowed favor on him before. It anchors Moses' later haste for divine pleasure and anger over the calf in a prior favor.

The addressee is told not to extend his eyes toward temporary worldly splendor; the Lord's provision is better and more lasting. It develops the eye and provision immediately after the praise-to-satisfaction command in 20:130.
Many beings prostrate to Allah, while many people deserve punishment and are humiliated by Him. It sets prostration beside the adverse judgment that cannot be honored away.
Those driven out for Allah's cause are admitted to an entrance they will be pleased with. It supplies a concrete, favorable entry for the language of rıza.
Allah has praise in the first and last life, and judgment belongs to Him. It brings حمد into the same final judgment horizon as the section's yawm.
Believers who act righteously are lodged in Garden chambers, and their reward is called نِعْمَ. The praise-form of the section's ni'ma judges their work favorably.
The faithful receive gardens as lodging for their deeds, while the defiantly disobedient have Fire as lodging. It mirrors the section's two end-groups without relying on the same root.
The man is described as one on whom Allah bestowed favor and on whom the Messenger bestowed favor. Its active grammar supplies a clear agent for an'amta-type benefaction.
After Job's trial, Allah calls him an excellent servant (نِعْمَ الْعَبْدُ). This applies the section's dictionary praise-form to a patient servant restored under divine judgment.
After the preceding scene of every community judged, all praise is assigned to Allah. It makes حمد the verbal seal of a differentiated Day.
Allah makes faith beloved and disbelief hateful, then calls the resulting people rightly guided. Together with 49:8's فضل and نعمة, it defines favor as an oriented heart.
Some sought Allah's رضوان through monasticism but did not observe it as required. It is a boundary case where intending rıza needs faithful completion.
The emigrants seek Allah's فضل and رضوان while supporting Allah and His Messenger. It shows rıza pursued through a concrete communal allegiance.
Hostile people bite their fingertips in rage when alone. It is an indirect bodily overflow of anger beside the section's facial and eye signs.
Covenant-breaking brings Allah's curse and hardens hearts. It gives a moral and inward counterpart to the wrath-side's adverse marking.
Every favor possessed is from Allah, and harm makes people call on Him. It states the gift-and-distress alternation underneath the section's two conditions.
They recognize Allah's favor and then deny it. The verse identifies refusal to acknowledge نعمة as a concrete turn away from the favorable response.
Allah's favor and mercy are said to be what makes purification possible. It gives the favorable side an inward cleansing rather than a facial sign.
The warning that scalding water sears faces is a plausible extension of the section's face under adverse judgment, though its own image is infernal heat rather than غضب or facial emotion.
Criminals are recognized by their marks before seizure. The link is limited to the section's concern that final judgment becomes legible on a person rather than remaining hidden.
When the true promise nears, disbelievers' eyes stare fixedly. This only indirectly relates to the section's eye imagery, but it is a specific eschatological eye-state.
Allah sees the Prophet turn his face toward heaven and gives him a qibla that will please him. It directly joins face-direction and rıza before 2:150 completes favor and guidance.
At death the angels strike the faces and backs of those who disbelieve and announce the burning punishment. It is a direct bodily mark of the adverse verdict.
The one Allah leaves astray is gathered on the Day upon his face, blind, mute, and deaf, with Hell as destination. It joins guidance versus straying to an overturned, sightless face.
After 19:58's favored people who fall prostrate, later successors neglect prayer, follow desire, and meet misguidance. It is the immediate contrary line of descent.
Those who are guided receive good speech and are guided to the path of the Praiseworthy (الحميد). It directly reunites the section's حمد with the straight-path image.
A Garden-dweller says that without his Lord's نعمة he would have been among those brought to punishment. Favor is what separates him from the adverse company.
Allah's curse makes them deaf and blinds their eyes. It gives the cursed, wrath-adjacent side a direct impairment of the eye.
A نعمة from Jonah's Lord reaches him so that he is not cast out blameworthy (مذموم). The verse explicitly sets favor against blame, the opposition developed for حمد in the section.
The righteous fear a Day described as frowning and severe (عبوسا قمطريرا). It supplies the grim facial vocabulary immediately before 76:11's radiance and joy.
The dust-darkened faces in 80:40–41 are identified as those of the disbelieving wicked. This ayah supplies the moral identity of that adverse facial scene.
When the Quran is recited to them, they do not prostrate. It is the direct reversal of 19:58 and 17:107–109, where reception of the signs brings faces to the ground.
The Lord will give to the addressee and he will be satisfied (فترضى). The ayah makes divine giving culminate in rıza.
The wording says Allah found the addressee ضالًّا and guided him. Whatever its exegetical scope, its own verbal pairing directly meets the section's guidance-versus-ضلّين concern.
Allah finds the addressee in need and makes him self-sufficient. It gives the gift-side of the section a concrete reversal of lack.
In the calf narrative, Moses calls his people to repentance, and Allah accepts it. This supplies a repentance route out of the calf episode whose wrath is explicit in 7:152.
Obedience to Allah and the Messenger would guide them to a straight path. It is the immediate path-condition before 4:69's company of those favored.
Believers are told not to forbid the good things Allah made lawful and not to transgress. It repeats 20:81's provision joined to a boundary against excess.
The next ayah commands eating the lawful, good provision Allah gives. Its own contribution is the gift whose misuse 5:87 forbids.
After taking the calf, they recognize that they have gone astray and appeal for mercy and forgiveness. It makes misguidance and hoped-for pardon explicit within the wrath narrative.
Moses asks forgiveness for himself and Aaron and asks to be admitted into mercy. The plea follows his angry return and opens the mercy side of the episode.
Yusuf is chosen, taught, and promised the completion of his Lord's favor upon him and Jacob's family. It shows نعمة arriving as election and understanding.
When Yusuf's shirt is placed over Jacob's face, Jacob's sight returns. This reverses the grief-altered eyes of 12:84, though its emotion is reunion rather than anger.
The revealed Book brings people from darkness into light and guides them to the path of the Mighty, Praiseworthy (الحميد). It gives the section's حمد a path-form.
After the gratitude-and-punishment division of 14:7, Moses calls Allah rich and praiseworthy. It distinguishes Allah's حمد from human gratitude or ingratitude.
Whoever is blind in this life is blind in the Hereafter and farther astray from the way. It connects the section's eye imagery to its lost-path side.
Those who repent, believe, and act righteously enter the Garden without injustice. It gives the recovery from 19:59's misguidance its own promised destination.
Allah says the people were tested after Moses and that the Samiri led them astray. It supplies the causal straying behind Moses' angry return in 20:86.
When guidance comes, whoever follows it will neither go astray nor be wretched. It gives the guided alternative to the fall under wrath in the same surah.
The one who turns from the reminder has a constricted life and is gathered blind on the Day. It gives straying a particular adverse eye-state.
Those given knowledge see the revelation as truth that guides to the path of the Mighty, Praiseworthy. It repeats the specific hamd-and-path meeting of 14:1 and 22:24.
Those who feed others say they seek neither recompense nor thanks from them. This gives 76:10–11's feared grim day and granted radiance an ethic that refuses human praise as payment.
The humbled faces are laboring and weary. Its own contribution contrasts exhausted labor with 88:9's face satisfied with its effort.
The laboring, humbled face enters a burning Fire. It supplies the immediate adverse destination for 88:2–3.
The soul addressed in 89:28 is first called tranquil. Its calmness is the inward inverse of the section's anger before the reciprocal rıza is named.
The charitable seeker of the Most High's face will soon be satisfied. It gives rıza as the outcome of an enacted favorable pursuit.
Allah finds the addressee an orphan and gives shelter. It is a concrete prior gift in the sequence whose later result is satisfaction in 93:5.
On that Day people will be questioned about نعيم. It turns the section's favorable gift into an accountable possession within its yawm horizon.
